examples.description: Prime p = 13 (the first uncovered residue class $p \equiv 1 \pmod{12)}$

examples.detail: For p=2473, one gets 4/2473 = 1/620 + 1/218240 + 1/33370609920. Indeed x=(p+7)/4=620, n=p(p+7)/4=1537660, and 7/n = 1/((n+20)/7) + 1/(n(n+20)/140) = 1/218240 + 1/33370609920. So this confirms the same pattern on the other residue class branch.

examples.description: Prime p = 337 (nearby comparison outside the new branch)
examples.detail: For p=337, a decomposition exists, for instance 4/337 = 1/87 + 1/2668 + 1/2697348. But the simpler x=(p+7)/4 pattern does not satisfy the same divisibility conditions as for p=313 or p=2473. This indicates the new family is narrower than all primes with $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$ and $p \equiv 3 \pmod{5}$.

For p=73, take x=(p+7)/4=20 and n=p(p+7)/4=1460. Then 4/p - 1/x = 7/n. Here n is divisible by 10 and $n \equiv 4 \pmod{7}$, so 7/n = 1/((n+10)/7) + 1/(n(n+10)/70) = 1/210 + 1/30660. Thus 4/73 = 1/20 + 1/210 + 1/30660. This shows the first certified x=(p+7)/4 branch is naturally stated in terms of n, not directly in terms of p.

For p=313, take x=(p+7)/4=80 and n=p(p+7)/4=25040. Again 4/p - 1/x = 7/n. This time n is divisible by 20 and $n \equiv 1 \pmod{7}$, so 7/n = 1/((n+20)/7) + 1/(n(n+20)/140) = 1/3580 + 1/4482160. Hence 4/313 = 1/80 + 1/3580 + 1/4482160. This is the second certified x=(p+7)/4 branch.

Also n is not divisible by 20, so the second umbrella condition fails as well. Thus the unified x=(p+7)/4 theorem does not explain the class $p \equiv 241 \pmod{840}$.

proof_attempts.sketch:
We can prove the conjecture for every prime p except possibly those with $p \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$.

1. The case p=2 is immediate: 4/2 = 1 + 1/2 + 1/2.

2. The case p=3 is also immediate: 4/3 = 1 + 1/4 + 1/12.

3. Now let p>3 be prime. Then p is odd and not divisible by 3, so p lies in one of the residue classes 1,5,7,11 modulo 12.

4. If $p \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$, define a=(p+1)/3, which is an integer. Then
   1/p + 1/a + 1/(pa)
   = 1/p + (p+1)/(pa)
   = 1/p + 3/p
   = 4/p.
   Hence every prime $p \equiv 5 or 11 \pmod{12}$ has a three-term Egyptian-fraction decomposition:
   4/p = 1/p + 1/((p+1)/3) + 1/(p(p+1)/3).

5. If $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, define b=(p+1)/4, which is an integer. Then
   1/b + 1/(2pb) + 1/(2pb)
   = 1/b + 1/(pb)
   = (p+1)/(pb)
   = 4/p.
   Hence every prime $p \equiv 7 or 11 \pmod{12}$ has a three-term decomposition:
   4/p = 1/((p+1)/4) + 1/(p(p+1)/2) + 1/(p(p+1)/2).

6. Combining the two cases: every prime p>3 with p 
$ot \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$ is covered. Therefore the original conjecture for primes reduces to the remaining class $p \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$.

This does not prove the full conjecture, because the class $p \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$ is still untreated.
proof_attempts.checker_feedback: Steps 1 and 2 are correct explicit decompositions for p=2 and p=3. In step 3, the residue-class statement is correct: every prime p>3 is odd and not divisible by 3, hence p mod 12 is in {1,5,7,11}. In step 4, if $p \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$, then a=(p+1)/3 is indeed an integer, and 1/a + 1/(pa) = (p+1)/(pa) = 3/p, so the displayed identity gives 4/p exactly. In step 5, if $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, then b=(p+1)/4 is an integer, and 1/(2pb)+1/(2pb)=1/(pb), so 1/b + 1/(pb) = (p+1)/(pb) = 4/p; this is also correct. Step 6 is therefore justified: the argument covers primes in classes 5,7,11 modulo 12, leaving only 1 modulo 12. This is a sound partial reduction, not a complete proof of the conjecture, so closes_conjecture must remain false.

proof_attempts.sketch:
We strengthen the previous valid reduction. The conjecture holds for every prime p except possibly those with $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$.

Start from the checked result PA-E552D9: every prime is already covered unless $p \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$. So it remains to treat primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$.

Now assume $p \equiv 13 \pmod{24}$. Then $p \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$, and in particular (p+3)/4 is an integer. Set

  x = (p+3)/4.

Then

  4/p - 1/x = 4/p - 4/(p+3) = 12/(p(p+3)).

Write

  n = p(p+3)/4.

Then the remainder is 3/n. Because $p \equiv 13 \pmod{24}$, we have $p+3 \equiv 16 \pmod{24}$, so (p+3)/4 is even; hence n = p(p+3)/4 is an even integer. Also $p \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ and $(p+3)/4 \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, so $n \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$.

For any even integer n with $n \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, we have the identity

  3/n = 1/((n+2)/3) + 1/(n(n+2)/6).

Indeed, since n is even and $n \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, both denominators are integers, and

  1/((n+2)/3) + 1/(n(n+2)/6)
  = 3/(n+2) + 6/(n(n+2))
  = (3n+6)/(n(n+2))
  = 3/n.

Therefore, for $p \equiv 13 \pmod{24}$, we obtain

  4/p = 1/((p+3)/4) + 1/((n+2)/3) + 1/(n(n+2)/6),

where n = p(p+3)/4. This is an explicit three-term Egyptian-fraction decomposition.

So combining with PA-E552D9, the conjecture is proved for all primes except possibly those with $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$.

Checks: for p=13, n=52, giving (x,y,z)=(4,18,468); for p=37, n=370, giving (10,124,22940).
proof_attempts.checker_feedback: The opening reduction to the class $p \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$ is already checker-validated via PA-E552D9, so it is legitimate to start from that point. For $p \equiv 13 \pmod{24}$, the choice x=(p+3)/4 is valid because p+3 is divisible by 4. The computation 4/p - 1/x = 4/p - 4/(p+3) = 12/(p(p+3)) is correct. Setting n=p(p+3)/4 rewrites the remainder as 3/n correctly. The parity claim is justified: if $p \equiv 13 \pmod{24}$, then p+$3 \equiv 16 \pmod{24}$, so (p+3)/4 is even, hence n is even. The congruence $n \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ is also correct because $p \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ and (p+3)/$4 \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$. The identity 3/n = 1/((n+2)/3) + 1/(n(n+2)/6) is verified by direct algebra, and the integrality conditions on both denominators follow from n even and $n \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$. Substituting this into the remainder therefore gives a valid explicit decomposition for every prime $p \equiv 13 \pmod{24}$. Consequently the argument soundly sharpens the unresolved residue class from $p \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$ to $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$. This is a genuine partial proof, not a complete proof of the full conjecture, so closes_conjecture remains false.

proof_attempts.sketch:
We record another explicit family inside the remaining difficult class.

Assume $p \equiv 97 \pmod{120}$. Then p is prime, $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$, and $p \equiv 2 \pmod{5}$.
Set

  x = (p+3)/4.

Since $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$, x is an integer. Then

  4/p - 1/x = 4/p - 4/(p+3) = 12/(p(p+3)).

Write

  n = p(p+3)/4.

Then the remainder is 3/n. Because $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$, we have $p \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ and $(p+3)/4 \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, so $n \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$. Because $p \equiv 2 \pmod{5}$, we have $p+3 \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$, hence n is divisible by 5.

For any integer n with $n \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ and 5 | n, we have the identity

  3/n = 1/((n+5)/3) + 1/(n(n+5)/15).

Indeed, the denominator (n+5)/3 is integral because $n \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, and n(n+5)/15 is integral because 5 | n and 3 | (n+5). Also

  1/((n+5)/3) + 1/(n(n+5)/15)
  = 3/(n+5) + 15/(n(n+5))
  = (3n+15)/(n(n+5))
  = 3/n.

Therefore, for every prime $p \equiv 97 \pmod{120}$,

  4/p = 1/((p+3)/4) + 1/((n+5)/3) + 1/(n(n+5)/15),

where n = p(p+3)/4.

Checks: p=97 gives (x,y,z)=(25,810,392850), and p=337 gives (85,9550,54711950). So the remaining class $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$ contains at least this further explicit subfamily.
proof_attempts.checker_feedback: The congruence assumptions are used correctly. From $p \equiv 97 \pmod{120}$, it follows that $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$, so x=(p+3)/4 is an integer. The computation 4/p - 1/x = 4/p - 4/(p+3) = 12/(p(p+3)) is correct, and with n=p(p+3)/4 this remainder is exactly 3/n. The claim $n \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ is justified because $p \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ and (p+3)/$4 \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, so their product is 1 modulo 3. The divisibility by 5 is also correct: $p \equiv 2 \pmod{5}$ implies p+$3 \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$, hence n is a multiple of 5. The identity 3/n = 1/((n+5)/3) + 1/(n(n+5)/15) is verified by direct algebra, and the integrality checks on both denominators are sufficient. Therefore the displayed construction yields a valid three-term decomposition for every prime $p \equiv 97 \pmod{120}$. This is a sound new partial family, but it does not cover all primes in the unresolved class $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$, so closes_conjecture remains false.

proof_attempts.sketch:
We prove another explicit family inside the remaining class $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$.

Assume p is a prime satisfying

  $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$,\qquad $p \equiv 3 \pmod{5}$,\qquad $p \equiv \pm 3 \pmod{7}$.

By the Chinese remainder theorem this is equivalent to $p \equiv 73 or 193 \pmod{840}$.

Set

  x = (p+7)/4.

Since $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$, x is an integer. Then

  4/p - 1/x = 4/p - 4/(p+7) = 28/(p(p+7)).

Write

  n = p(p+7)/4.

Then the remainder is 7/n.

We now verify the divisibility conditions needed to split 7/n into two unit fractions.

1. Because $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$, we have $p+7 \equiv 8 \pmod{24}$, so (p+7)/4 is even. Hence n is even.

2. Because $p \equiv 3 \pmod{5}$, we have $p+7 \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$, so n is divisible by 5. Combining with (1), n is divisible by 10.

3. Modulo 7, since p+7 \equiv p, we have

   n = p(p+7)/4 \equiv $p^{2}$/4 \pmod{7}.

   Because $4^{-1} \equiv 2 \pmod{7}$, this gives $n \equiv 2p^{2} \pmod{7}$. If $p \equiv \pm 3 \pmod{7}$, then $p^{2} \equiv 2 \pmod{7}$, so $n \equiv 4 \pmod{7}$. Hence $n+10 \equiv 0 \pmod{7}$.

Therefore the quantities

  y = (n+10)/7, \qquad z = n(n+10)/70

are positive integers. Moreover,

  1/y + 1/z
  = 7/(n+10) + 70/(n(n+10))
  = (7n+70)/(n(n+10))
  = 7/n.

Substituting back, we obtain the identity

  4/p = 1/((p+7)/4) + 1/((n+10)/7) + 1/(n(n+10)/70),

where n = p(p+7)/4.

Hence the conjecture holds for every prime $p \equiv 73 or 193 \pmod{840}$. This gives another explicit subfamily inside the unresolved class $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$.

  4/p - 1/x = 4/p - 4/(p+7) = 28/(p(p+7)) = 7/n.

So every decomposition produced by this method reduces to expressing 7/n as a sum of two unit fractions.

We now prove two general identities.

Case 1. Suppose 10 divides n and $n \equiv 4 \pmod{7}$. Then n+10 is divisible by 7, and the quantities

  y = (n+10)/7, \qquad z = n(n+10)/70

are integers. Moreover,

  1/y + 1/z
  = 7/(n+10) + 70/(n(n+10))
  = (7n+70)/(n(n+10))
  = 7/n.

Hence in this case

  4/p = 1/x + 1/((n+10)/7) + 1/(n(n+10)/70).

Case 2. Suppose 20 divides n and $n \equiv 1 \pmod{7}$. Then n+20 is divisible by 7, and the quantities

  y = (n+20)/7, \qquad z = n(n+20)/140

are integers. Also,

  1/y + 1/z
  = 7/(n+20) + 140/(n(n+20))
  = (7n+140)/(n(n+20))
  = 7/n.

Hence in this case

  4/p = 1/x + 1/((n+20)/7) + 1/(n(n+20)/140).

Therefore we obtain the following umbrella statement:

  If $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$, x=(p+7)/4, n=p(p+7)/4, and either
  (i) 10 | n with $n \equiv 4 \pmod{7}$, or
  (ii) 20 | n with $n \equiv 1 \pmod{7}$,
